questions.question: A SOC analyst pulls a search returning duplicate events that share the same `src_ip` and `dest_port`. They want ONE event per unique (src_ip, dest_port) pair, keeping the first occurrence. Which SPL command does this?
options: `dedup src_ip, dest_port` — removes subsequent duplicates for that key
`unique src_ip, dest_port` — no `unique` command exists in core SPL
`distinct src_ip, dest_port` — no `distinct` command exists in core SPL
`deduplicate src_ip, dest_port` — no `deduplicate` command exists in core SPL
questions.explanation: `dedup <fields>` removes duplicate events based on the specified field values, keeping the first (or first N with `dedup N field`). `unique`, `distinct`, and `deduplicate` are not core SPL commands — they are common name-guesses drawn from other query languages (SQL `DISTINCT`, Python `unique`, etc.), but Splunk uses `dedup` exclusively for this job.

questions.question: A Splunk admin runs `index=main | stats count by host`. What does this exact pipeline return?
options: The total number of events in `index=main` as a single number
A count of events grouped by the `host` field, one row per host
The number of distinct hosts as a single number
All events in the index with `host` as the sort key
questions.explanation: `stats count by host` is a transforming command: it returns one row per distinct `host` with a `count` column. Option A (a single grand total) would be `stats count` with no `by`. Option C (distinct host count) would be `stats dc(host)`. Option D (returning all events sorted) is not what any `stats` clause does — `stats` collapses events into aggregates.

questions.question: An SPL search must match events where `status` is 404 OR 500. Which SPL syntax is a valid single-field OR match?
options: `status=404 status=500` — implicit AND, not OR
`status BETWEEN 404 AND 500` — no `BETWEEN` operator in SPL
`status IN (404, 500)`
`status=[404,500]` — array literal is not valid SPL match syntax
questions.explanation: `status IN (404, 500)` (added in Splunk 6.3) matches events where `status` equals any listed value — equivalent to `status=404 OR status=500`. Adjacent `field=value` pairs (option A) are implicitly ANDed together, so no event has status equal to both. Splunk SPL has no `BETWEEN` operator (C) — numeric range comparisons use `where`. Array-literal syntax `[404,500]` (D) is not part of Splunk's search language.

questions.question: After a search, an analyst wants the result column `src_ip` to display as `SourceIP` (rename only, no data change). Which SPL command does this?
options: `| fields src_ip AS SourceIP` — `fields` selects columns, no rename
`| alias src_ip AS SourceIP` — no top-level `alias` command in SPL
`| convert src_ip AS SourceIP` — `convert` changes value types, not names
`| rename src_ip AS SourceIP` — the `rename` command renames fields
questions.explanation: `rename <old> AS <new>` renames a field in-pipeline. `fields` (A) chooses which columns are carried forward but cannot rename them. There is no `| alias` SPL command (B) — field aliases exist as a knowledge object in `Settings → Fields → Field Aliases`, not as an inline pipeline command. `convert` (D) coerces string values into numeric or time types (e.g. `convert num(bytes)`), not for renaming.

questions.question: An SPL search computes a new field: `... | eval response_kb = response_bytes / 1024`. Which best describes the `eval` command?
options: It filters events matching a boolean condition and drops non-matches
It creates or overwrites fields using math, string, or boolean expressions
It executes external scripts against each event via the OS shell
It compiles panel expressions for dashboard display at render time
questions.explanation: `eval` computes an expression and stores the result in a new or existing field on every event — the core mechanism for search-time derived fields. Option A describes `where` (or the `search` command mid-pipeline). Option C describes scripted lookups or the `run` command in older versions, not `eval`. Option D confuses `eval` with Simple XML dashboard token expressions that only run at UI render time.

questions.question: An analyst needs `earliest` to mean 'the beginning (00:00:00) of the current day'. Splunk time modifiers use `@` to snap to the start of a unit. Which value fits?
options: `earliest=-1d` — 24 hours ago, not the start of today
`earliest=now/d` — `/d` is not valid snap syntax in SPL
`earliest=@d`
`earliest=0d` — treated as 'now', not midnight today
questions.explanation: In Splunk time modifiers, `@<unit>` snaps to the START of that unit. `@d` = 00:00 of the current day. `-1d` (A) is a rolling 24-hour offset from now. `now/d` (B) uses `/` which is not a Splunk snap operator. `0d` (C) is interpreted as no offset — equivalent to `now` — not midnight.

questions.question: An analyst is choosing between `chart` and `timechart`. Which statement correctly describes `timechart`?
options: `timechart` can plot categorical values on the X-axis when `by` is omitted
`timechart` supports more aggregation functions than `chart` does
`timechart` requires an explicit `over` clause to designate the X-axis field
`timechart` always uses `_time` as the X-axis and creates time bins automatically
questions.explanation: `timechart` is a specialisation of `chart` with `_time` fixed as the X-axis; span/binning is automatic based on the search's time range. Option B is wrong — the aggregation function set is essentially the same for both. Option C describes `chart` (which accepts `over <field>`); `timechart` does not take an `over` clause. Option A contradicts the definition: `timechart` always uses `_time`, never a categorical X.

questions.question: An analyst wants the TOP 10 most common values of the `user_agent` field with count and percent. Which single SPL command produces that?
options: `top user_agent` — returns most common values with count and percent
`rare user_agent` — returns the LEAST common values (opposite direction)
`stats top(user_agent)` — `top()` is not a valid `stats` function
`sort user_agent` — sorts events, does not aggregate counts or percents
questions.explanation: `top <field>` is a transforming command that returns the most frequent values with `count` and `percent` columns, defaulting to 10. `rare` (B) does the exact opposite — least common. `stats top(...)` (C) is invalid; `stats` supports `count`, `values`, `dc`, etc., but not `top()`. `sort` (D) reorders events but does not compute frequencies.

questions.question: Splunk search has three modes: Fast, Smart (default), and Verbose. Which pair correctly matches modes to behaviour?
options: Smart forces field discovery on every search regardless of command type
Fast is limited to indexers; Verbose is limited to heavy forwarders
Fast disables field discovery for maximum speed; Verbose discovers all fields
Verbose disables event rendering to save memory on the search head
questions.explanation: Fast disables field discovery / event rendering for speed. Verbose builds all fields, event types, and tags — the richest, slowest mode. Smart (the default) auto-switches: if the search has a transforming command it behaves like Fast; otherwise like Verbose. Option B mixes modes with tier roles arbitrarily. Option A is the opposite of Smart's actual behaviour (Smart skips discovery when transforming commands are present). Option D describes Fast, not Verbose.

questions.question: An analyst needs to parameterise a search using the result of another search — e.g. filter to `src_ip` values returned by a separate lookup search. Which describes Splunk subsearch syntax and semantics?
options: Written after the main search with `| join`; runs after the main search
Written as `subsearch(name)` and streams to a new tab in the UI
Referenced by name after `sourcetype=` in the main search
Enclosed in square brackets `[...]`; runs first, results become filter terms
questions.explanation: A subsearch is enclosed in `[ ... ]`; it runs first and its rows are converted into a filter that is spliced into the outer search. Option A confuses subsearch with the `join` command (which is a different pattern and runs after the main results). Option C invents non-existent syntax. Option B is not real — subsearch is not a UI feature. Note the default 60-second / 10 000-result subsearch cap.

questions.question: An analyst wants to add a new field holding the character length of the `url` string. Which eval function returns the character count of a string?
options: `len(url)` — Splunk eval string-length function
`strlen(url)` — not an eval function in Splunk SPL
`length(url)` — not an eval function in Splunk SPL
`count(url)` — a `stats` aggregator, not an eval string function
questions.explanation: Splunk's eval string-length function is `len()`. `length()` and `strlen()` (A, B) are name-guesses borrowed from other languages — neither exists in Splunk eval. `count()` (D) is a stats aggregator that counts events, not a string function usable in `eval`. Prior versions of this question incorrectly marked `length()` correct; `len()` is the only right answer.

questions.question: An analyst wants to extract a field `user` from raw event text containing `user=alice@example.com` using `rex` at search time. Which SPL syntax is correct?
options: `rex extract user from "user=<user>"`
`rex field=_raw "user=(?<user>[^\s]+)"`
`rex "user=(?P<user>[^\s]+)"` — `(?P<name>)` is Python regex, not Splunk
`rex "user" as user field=_raw` — invalid `rex` argument ordering
questions.explanation: Splunk's `rex` uses PCRE named-capture syntax `(?<name>pattern)`. `field=_raw` is the default and can be omitted. Option A invents `extract ... from` syntax that Splunk does not have. Option C uses Python's `(?P<name>...)` form — Splunk accepts `(?<name>...)` only. Option D is not a valid `rex` invocation; there is no `"regex" as fieldname` form.

questions.question: An admin sets up an alert: 'fire when the count of failed logins from a single IP exceeds 10 in any 15-minute window' using `stats count by src_ip | where count > 10`. Which trigger-condition setting fits?
options: Number of events > 10 — counts raw events, not the aggregated rows
Number of sources > 0 — 'sources' means `source` field, not result rows
Number of hosts > 10 — wrong dimension (hosts, not src_ip rows)
Number of results > 0 — fires whenever a row survives `where count > 10`
questions.explanation: Because the search transforms events into a per-src_ip table and pre-filters with `where count > 10`, ANY row that survives is already a violation — so the alert trigger 'Number of results > 0' fires exactly when needed. Option A operates on raw event count, ignoring aggregation. Options C and D bind the trigger to unrelated dimensions (`host`, `source`) that have nothing to do with unique IPs above threshold.

questions.question: An analyst wants to enrich search results with data from an external CSV `asset_owners.csv`, joining on a key field, and also to list the CSV contents directly. Which pair of features fits?
options: A lookup definition for the enrichment; `inputlookup` to load CSV rows into the pipeline
A field alias for the enrichment; `metadata` command to list the CSV rows
An event type for the enrichment; `outputlookup` to load CSV rows into the pipeline
A tag for the enrichment; `dbxquery` to load CSV rows into the pipeline
questions.explanation: Lookups enrich events with external data (CSV, KV Store, geo, DB) by matching a key. `inputlookup <table>` reads the lookup table into the pipeline as rows. A field alias (A) just renames existing fields, not an enrichment; `metadata` inspects indexes, not lookup files. An event type (C) categorises events by search, not by external data; `outputlookup` writes to a lookup, not reads. Tags (D) label field=value pairs; `dbxquery` is the DB Connect app's SQL runner, not a CSV reader.

questions.question: An automatic lookup is configured in `Settings → Lookups → Automatic Lookups`. What does it do?
options: Refreshes the underlying CSV file from an external source on the lookup's own schedule
Applies the lookup silently to searches whose events contain the input field
Writes new rows into the lookup file automatically when events introduce new key values
Forwards lookup output back to the indexers to be re-ingested as new indexed events
questions.explanation: An automatic lookup silently applies the mapping at search time whenever an event contains the lookup's input field — no `| lookup` needed in the SPL. Option A confuses automatic lookups with KV Store collection refresh or a scheduled `outputlookup` job. Option C is wrong — lookups are read-only from the search side; new rows require an explicit `outputlookup`. Option D is not a Splunk feature at all.

questions.question: In `stats`, two functions aggregate the values of a field. Which correctly contrasts `values()` and `list()`?
options: `values()` keeps duplicates and preserves order; `list()` deduplicates and sorts
`values()` and `list()` produce byte-for-byte identical output in every case
`values()` dedups + sorts values; `list()` keeps duplicates and order
`values()` returns only the field's first value; `list()` returns only its last value
questions.explanation: `values(field)` returns the DISTINCT values (deduplicated), sorted lexicographically. `list(field)` returns EVERY value in the order it appeared, including duplicates. Option B contradicts the documentation. Option A swaps their behaviour — `values` dedups, `list` doesn't. Option D confuses these aggregators with `first()` / `last()`, which return a single value each.

questions.question: A search `index=web | stats avg(bytes) AS avg_bytes BY status` returns `status=200 avg_bytes=15234`. What does that row mean?
options: The average response size for status=200 events was 15,234 bytes
Status 200 occurred 15,234 times in the search window
The median response size for status=200 events was 15,234 bytes
The maximum response size for a status=200 event was 15,234 bytes
questions.explanation: `avg(bytes)` is the arithmetic mean of `bytes` per group. Grouped by `status`, the row for `status=200` reports the mean `bytes` value across those events. Option B describes `count`, not `avg`. Option C describes the `median()` function. Option D describes `max()`. Each produces a different aggregate — only `avg()` matches the query.

questions.question: An analyst wants the FIRST 20 events from a search (in returned order, before any sort). Which SPL command does this?
options: `limit 20` — no `limit` command in core SPL (subsearch has a limit argument)
`head 20` — returns the first 20 events in pipeline order
`top 20` — returns the top 20 by frequency of a field, not first N events
`first 20` — no `first` command in core SPL
questions.explanation: `head N` returns the first N events. `tail N` is the mirror image. `limit` (B) is not a core SPL command — it appears only as an argument in a few commands like `top limit=N`. `top 20` (C) is a frequency aggregator, not a first-N slice. `first` (D) is only an eval/stats function (`first()`), not a pipeline command.

questions.question: An admin wants `clientip` to also be queryable as `src_ip` so legacy dashboards keep working. Which knowledge object provides this at search time?
options: Calculated field — computes a new value from an eval expression
Event type — categorises events by a saved search
Field alias — maps one field name to another at search time
Tag — labels a specific field=value pair
questions.explanation: A field alias (`Settings → Fields → Field Aliases`) creates an alternative name for an existing field, applied per source type at search time. Event types (B) categorise events matching a search — they add an `eventtype` value, not a field alias. Calculated fields (C) run an `eval` to derive a new value; they do not create name aliases. Tags (D) label specific `field=value` pairs, not fields themselves.

questions.question: An analyst writes `index=web | stats dc(user_agent)`. What does `dc()` do?
options: Sums numeric values of the field — that's `sum()`
Averages numeric values of the field — that's `avg()`
Concatenates all values of the field into one string
Counts the DISTINCT values seen for the field
questions.explanation: `dc(field)` (alias `distinct_count`) counts unique values of a field across the grouped events. Option A is `sum()`. Option B is `avg()`. Option C is `mvjoin()` or `values()` combined with `mvjoin()` — not `dc()`. `dc()` is often confused with `count()`, but `count()` counts events, not distinct values.

questions.question: A SOC wants to categorise events at search time via a saved search expression (e.g. `index=fw action=blocked` → `firewall_deny`). Which knowledge object does this?
options: Tag — labels field values, not events matching a search
Event type — a saved search expression that categorises matching events
Field extraction — pulls new fields from raw text, not categorisation
Workflow action — a right-click UI link, not a saved category
questions.explanation: An event type is a saved search that categorises any matching event by attaching an `eventtype` value. Tags (A) label individual field=value pairs and are commonly applied ON TOP of event types, but they do not use a search expression themselves. Field extractions (C) generate new fields from raw text. Workflow actions (D) are UI-level click-throughs from a field value to an external system.

questions.question: Tags and event types are related knowledge objects. Which correctly describes both?
options: Tags apply system-wide always; event types only apply within a single dashboard panel
Tags apply at index-time only; event types apply at search-time only, never earlier
Tags label specific field=value pairs; event types categorise events by a saved search
Tags depend on a CSV lookup file; event types depend on a KV Store collection to work
questions.explanation: A tag is a label attached to a specific `field=value` pair (e.g. tagging `sourcetype=access_combined` with 'web'). An event type is a categorisation saved as a search — matching events pick up an `eventtype` value. Tags may then be applied to event types. Option B is wrong — both are search-time constructs. Option A is invented. Option D confuses them with lookup / KV Store enrichment, which is a separate mechanism.

questions.question: A reusable SPL fragment `failed_logins(index)` should expand `\`failed_logins(security)\`` to `index=security action=failure`. Which macro definition is correct?
options: `index=@index@ action=failure` with argument count = 1
`index=${index} action=failure` with argument count = 1
`index=%index% action=failure` with argument count = 1
`index=$index$ action=failure` with argument count = 1
questions.explanation: Splunk search macros use `$argname$` delimiters for arguments — nothing else. Options B (`${..}`), C (`%..%`), and D (`@..@`) are all borrowed from shell, template engines, or other languages — none work in Splunk macro definitions. The macro is invoked with backticks: `` `failed_logins(security)` ``.

questions.question: An SPL `chart count BY status OVER host` builds a 2-D matrix. What role does the field named in the `over` clause play?
options: Defines the X-axis (rows in the resulting table)
Restricts the time range for the chart
Sets the maximum number of series returned by the chart
Determines the sort order of the resulting rows
questions.explanation: In `chart`, `over <field>` specifies the row (X-axis) field and `by <field>` specifies the column series. So `over host` produces one row per host. Option C describes the `limit` argument, which caps series and rolls the rest into 'OTHER'. Option B is set by `earliest`/`latest`, not `over`. Option D is `sort`; `over` doesn't sort.

questions.question: SPL has two filtering primitives: `search` and `where`. Which describes `where` correctly?
options: Runs before events are retrieved, at the indexer bloom-filter stage
Filters using keyword and `field=value` matches only, like the initial search
Filters using eval-style boolean expressions, including comparisons between fields
Is deprecated in favour of `| eval` in modern Splunk versions
questions.explanation: `where` accepts eval-style expressions, so it can compare fields to each other (`where bytes > avg_bytes`) or use functions like `like()`. Option A describes the initial `search` clause, which is what actually pushes down to indexers. Option B is exactly what `search` does — not `where`. Option D is wrong: `where` remains fully supported and is often required for post-aggregation filtering.

questions.question: An admin wants Splunk to tail `/var/log/auth.log` on a Linux host and forward new lines to the indexer. Which input type in `inputs.conf` is correct?
options: Scripted input: `[script:///opt/scripts/tail.sh]`
TCP input: `[tcp://514]`
HTTP Event Collector: `[http://splunk:8088]`
File monitor input: `[monitor:///var/log/auth.log]`
questions.explanation: `[monitor://path]` is the file-tailing input, typically deployed via a Universal Forwarder. `[tcp://...]` (B) receives network senders (syslog, etc.); it doesn't watch a local file. HEC (C) is an HTTP-POST endpoint for apps — the stanza syntax shown is wrong anyway (HEC is configured via `inputs.conf` `[http]` plus tokens, not a URL). Scripted inputs (D) execute a script on a schedule; useful for data a script generates, not for tailing a log file.

questions.question: An app team wants to push events to Splunk over HTTPS with a token — no forwarder installed. Which Splunk feature enables this?
options: HTTP Event Collector (HEC) — POST to `/services/collector` with a token
REST API `saved/searches` — used for saved-search management, not raw ingest
Universal Forwarder in agentless mode — no such agentless mode exists
TCP input on port 9997 — indexer replication port, not a public app-ingest path
questions.explanation: HEC receives JSON events over HTTPS at `/services/collector` using token authentication — no forwarder needed. Option B is a REST endpoint for managing saved searches, not ingesting events. Option C is fictional — the UF is by definition an agent. Option D is the port indexers use to receive forwarder traffic; it is not a general app-ingest API and requires forwarder framing.

questions.question: Scheduled reports and alerts are related. Which describes their relationship correctly?
options: Alerts run only in real time; scheduled reports run on cron and never in real time
Both are scheduled; alerts add a trigger condition and fire actions when it is met
Scheduled reports fire actions on completion; alerts merely save their results to disk
Alerts always write results to a CSV lookup; scheduled reports only render in dashboards
questions.explanation: A scheduled report runs on a cron schedule and produces results. An alert is a scheduled search PLUS a trigger condition (e.g. `number of results > 0`) that fires notifications, scripts, webhooks, etc. Option A is wrong — alerts can be scheduled OR real-time; scheduled reports likewise use cron. Options C and D swap or invent behaviour that neither object has.

questions.question: A knowledge-engineering team needs to create AND share saved searches, lookups, and dashboards within their app — but not manage users or system settings. Which default role fits?
options: User — can save private objects but cannot share app-wide
Can Read — read-only role with no creation rights
Admin — can do this, but grants far more than needed
Power User
questions.explanation: Power User is the default role that grants creation AND sharing of knowledge objects at the app scope, without full admin access. User (A) can create objects but only save them privately. Can Read (B) is read-only. Admin (C) satisfies the requirement but massively over-privileges the team, violating least-privilege. Power User is the target role for the Splunk Core Certified Power User exam.

questions.question: Splunk knowledge-object sharing has three scopes: Private, App, and Global. Which describes App vs Global correctly?
options: App = visible to all users of a specific app; Global = visible across every app
App = visible only to the object's creator; Global = visible to their role peers
App and Global are synonyms — both make the object visible everywhere in Splunk
App = objects manageable via REST only; Global = objects manageable via UI only
questions.explanation: Private means only the creator sees the object. App restricts visibility to users of a specific app (`search`, `enterprise_security`, etc.). Global exposes the object across every app to anyone with the required role. Option B conflates them. Option C inverts the meanings. Option D confuses sharing scope with the transport used to manage the object.

questions.question: In the pipeline `index=web | fields user_agent, status, bytes`, what does `fields user_agent, status, bytes` do?
options: Drops events where any of the three listed fields is missing or empty
Keeps only those fields (plus internal fields), reducing memory downstream
Sorts events by the three listed fields left-to-right in ascending order
Renames the three listed fields to canonical Splunk internal names
questions.explanation: `fields <list>` is a positive projection: only the listed fields (plus `_time`, `_raw`, `_indextime`, etc.) are carried forward. `fields - <list>` is the negative form. Option A describes what `where isnotnull(field)` or `search field=*` would do. Option C is `sort`. Option D is `rename`. Only projection matches `fields`.

questions.question: A dashboard panel must show event count by sourcetype over the last 24 hours and auto-refresh every 5 minutes. The team prefers relative-time historical searches over real-time. Which approach fits?
options: A real-time 24-hour window with a 5-minute refresh — expensive and unnecessary
A one-off ad-hoc search re-run manually by the user
A historical search with `earliest=-24h latest=now` and a 5-minute panel refresh
A summary-indexing job that writes to `main` every minute
questions.explanation: Historical relative-time searches (`earliest=-24h latest=now`) plus a 5-minute panel auto-refresh give a rolling 24-hour view at low cost. Option A uses real-time, which continuously evaluates and is resource-intensive — the opposite of the requirement. Option B is not a solution, just manual reruns. Option D pollutes `main` (never write summary data there) and is far heavier than needed for a simple 24-hour panel.

questions.question: An admin defines `EVAL-response_ms = response_ns / 1000000` in `props.conf` so every matching event gains the field at search time — no data rewrite. Which feature is this?
options: Calculated field
Index-time field extraction — modifies data during indexing
Field alias — renames an existing field
Automatic lookup — enriches from an external table
questions.explanation: A calculated field applies an `eval` expression at search time to every event of a matching sourcetype, without touching indexed data. Option B is wrong — the point of a calculated field is that it runs at SEARCH time, not index time. Option C only renames a field, it does not compute. Option D reads from an external table (CSV / KV Store), which is not what a plain `eval` expression does.

questions.question: An ES admin wants to normalise field names across firewall, VPN, endpoint, and auth sources so one SPL query works everywhere (`src_ip`, `user`, `action`, ...). Which Splunk framework provides this?
options: Common Event Format (CEF) — a vendor-neutral log wire format, not a Splunk framework
Common Information Model (CIM) — a shared semantic schema and data models
Splunk Enterprise Security data lake — a product, not a normalisation framework
Universal Forwarder templates — configure ingestion, not field semantics
questions.explanation: The Splunk CIM is a shared semantic model shipped as an add-on: canonical field names and data models per domain (Authentication, Network Traffic, Web, etc.), used by ES and premium apps. Option A (CEF) is an Arcsight/Micro Focus event format, not a Splunk knowledge framework. Options C and D are unrelated — one is a product, the other is ingestion tooling.

questions.question: A 90-day `stats count by src_ip` over firewall data is slow because it reads raw events. Accelerating the underlying data model builds summary indexes. Which SPL command reads those summaries?
options: `summary` — no such SPL command
`accelerate` — no such SPL command
`tstats`
`fast` — no such SPL command
questions.explanation: `tstats` queries accelerated data-model summaries and indexed tsidx files, bypassing raw events for orders-of-magnitude speed-ups. It uses full data-model paths, e.g. `tstats count from datamodel=Authentication by Authentication.user`. Options B, C, D are name-guesses — none exist as SPL commands. Data-model acceleration is configured on the data model itself; `tstats` is the read side.

questions.question: An analyst wants to group related events into a single transaction (e.g. all events sharing `JSESSIONID`, within a 30-min idle gap). What does `transaction` do, and what's the trade-off?
options: Orchestrates multi-step business processes across a chain of saved searches over time
Provides ACID guarantees for multi-event writes performed against the Splunk index
Runs a KV-store atomic multi-row write across the specified fields for the events
Groups related events by shared field / time gap; heavy on high-cardinality data
questions.explanation: `transaction` groups events sharing a field (or time constraint) into one record, adding `duration` and `eventcount`. It is powerful but memory-heavy — `stats` is preferred when only aggregation is needed. Option B invents write-side ACID semantics; Splunk indexes are write-once/append-only, not transactional. Option C mixes `transaction` with KV Store CRUD, which is unrelated. Option A describes orchestration frameworks, not this command.

questions.question: Two ways to define a field extraction in Splunk: inline `EXTRACT-<name>` in `props.conf`, and `TRANSFORMS-<class>` pointing to a stanza in `transforms.conf`. Which describes the pair correctly?
options: Both run at index-time; they differ only in file location and stanza naming
Inline is search-time; TRANSFORMS unlocks SOURCE_KEY, FORMAT, MV_ADD, REPEAT_MATCH
Inline runs at search-time; TRANSFORMS runs at index-time only
Inline is defined via the `rex` SPL command; TRANSFORMS uses the `erex` command
questions.explanation: Both live at search time. Inline `EXTRACT-` is compact — one regex per stanza in `props.conf`. `TRANSFORMS-<class>` in `props.conf` references a stanza in `transforms.conf` (via `REGEX` / `FORMAT`) and unlocks features like `SOURCE_KEY`, format templates, `MV_ADD`, and `REPEAT_MATCH`. Option A is wrong — neither is index-time. Option C reverses the truth. Option D confuses `.conf` extractions with SPL commands.

questions.question: An analyst runs `| makeresults | eval test="hello world" | rex field=test "(?<word>\w+)"`. How many rows does the final pipeline return, and what is in `word`?
options: 0 rows because `rex` fails when the pattern matches multiple times
2 rows, `word` becomes a multivalue with both matches
1 row, `word="hello"`
1 row, `word="hello world"` — `rex` returns the whole matched text
questions.explanation: By default `rex` extracts only the FIRST match into the named field, leaving row count unchanged. To capture all matches into a multivalue field, use `max_match=0`. Option B is wrong without that flag. Option A is a myth — `rex` never drops rows on match count. Option D would only be true if the regex were `.*` and greedy — `(?<word>\w+)` matches only up to the first whitespace.

questions.question: An event has `status=503`. `eval status_label = case(status>=500, "Error", status>=400, "Client Error", status>=200, "Success")` — `case` stops at the first true condition. What does `status_label` become?
options: "Success" — first-match wins is the wrong order
null — multiple conditions match so `case` returns null
"Client Error" — the second condition matches
"Error" — first condition `status>=500` matches 503
questions.explanation: `case()` evaluates arguments in pairs left-to-right and returns the first matching branch's value. 503 satisfies `status>=500` (which is listed first), so `status_label = "Error"`. Option A reverses the evaluation direction. Option C would be true only if `status>=500` came later. Option B invents behaviour: `case()` never returns null on multi-match — it just picks the first.

questions.question: Every event with a `host` field should be enriched at search time with owner and criticality from a KV Store collection `cmdb_hosts`, without typing `| lookup` each time. Which feature fits?
options: Automatic lookup pointing at the KV Store collection
Data-model acceleration on `cmdb_hosts`
A workflow action defined on `host`
A subsearch reading from `cmdb_hosts` on every search
questions.explanation: Automatic lookups (Settings → Lookups → Automatic Lookups) attach lookup output fields to every matching event, whether the lookup source is a CSV or a KV Store collection. Option B accelerates data-model queries (`tstats`), not per-event enrichment. Option C creates a right-click UI action, not an automatic per-event join. Option D is a manual pattern; it does not enrich automatically for all searches.

questions.question: A pipeline `| sort -count` orders results by `count` descending. Which best describes `sort` in Splunk?
options: Orders results by a relevance score computed from token frequency in `_raw`
Orders results by `_time` newest-first regardless of the field name supplied
Orders results by the specified field; ascending by default; `-` prefix reverses
Orders results randomly to bootstrap statistical sampling of the population
questions.explanation: `sort` orders results by one or more fields; ascending by default; `-field` for descending. `sort 0 -count` removes the default 10 000-result cap. Option B describes the initial default event order in Splunk Web (newest first), not the `sort` command's semantics. Option A invents a relevance model. Option D is `eval rnd=random() | sort rnd`, not what `sort` alone does.

questions.question: In a search result, right-clicking `src_ip` shows menu items 'Open in CMDB', 'Block IP via Firewall API'. These are pre-configured interactive links registered against fields or event types. Which knowledge object is this?
options: Scheduled report — cron-fired, not click-driven
Alert action — action fired when an alert triggers, not on right-click
Data model attribute — schema element, not an interactive UI menu
Workflow action — interactive per-field hyperlinks and POST actions
questions.explanation: Workflow actions add clickable per-field hyperlinks or POST form submissions in search results, letting analysts pivot to external systems or run follow-up searches with the field pre-filled. Option B are actions triggered by alert conditions — different life cycle. Option C is a data-model concept, not a UI object. Option A fires on cron, never on user interaction.

questions.question: An alert fires on every 5-minute schedule and spams the ops team. The admin enables `throttle: suppress for 1 hour by src_ip`. What does throttling do?
options: Suppresses re-firing of the alert for a time window, optionally per field value
Reduces the alert search's cron frequency
Limits the number of result rows via `head`-style truncation
Delays the initial trigger until a minimum number of matches accumulate
questions.explanation: Throttling prevents an alert from re-firing for a configured window after it fires, optionally scoped to a field value (so alerts are per-src_ip). This is the standard remedy for alert fatigue on persistent conditions. Option B changes schedule cadence, not throttling. Option C caps result rows, unrelated to firing. Option D describes the trigger threshold itself (e.g. 'number of results > N'), not throttling.

questions.question: A dashboard exposes a text input where users type a hostname. The panel search uses `index=main host=$host_input$`. The `$...$` placeholder is a dashboard-level variable that updates panels when changed. What is this variable called?
options: HEC token — authentication token for HTTP Event Collector
Token — dashboard variable referenced with `$name$`
REST API key — credential for `splunkd` REST endpoints
Session cookie — browser-side login state
questions.explanation: Splunk dashboards use TOKENS as the variable primitive: inputs set them, panel searches read them via `$token$`. Option A is an unrelated auth token used to POST events to HEC. Option C is a per-user credential for the REST API. Option D is browser state, not a dashboard variable. Only 'token' names the correct concept.

questions.question: A scheduled saved search computes daily aggregates and persists results to `daily_totals.csv`, later read via `| inputlookup daily_totals.csv`. Which SPL command writes the pipeline's current results into the lookup?
options: `| collect index=summary` — writes to a summary index, not to a lookup file
`| dumpresults daily_totals` — no such SPL command
`| outputcsv daily_totals` — no such SPL command
`| outputlookup daily_totals.csv` — writes current results to a lookup
questions.explanation: `outputlookup` writes the current search results to a CSV or KV Store lookup, replacing (or appending, with `append=t`) the target. Option A is the summary-indexing command — it appends events to a summary index, not to a lookup file. Options C and D are name-guesses; neither exists in SPL. Note: `outputlookup` requires write permission on the lookup definition.

questions.question: A multivalue field `tags = ['prod','db','primary']`. To extract the SECOND element (0-based index 1), the analyst uses an eval function. Which one?
options: `mvindex(tags, 1)` — returns the value at zero-based index 1
`mvget(tags, 1)` — no such eval function in Splunk
`tags[1]` — bracket indexing is not valid eval syntax in SPL
`getmv(tags, 1)` — no such eval function in Splunk
questions.explanation: `mvindex(field, start[, end])` extracts a value or slice from a multivalue field by position; negative indices count from the end. Options B and D are name-guesses that don't exist in Splunk eval. Option C uses `[index]` bracket syntax, which is valid in Python and JavaScript but not in Splunk SPL — SPL requires the function form.

questions.question: An ingest stanza sets no `sourcetype`. How does Splunk decide the sourcetype at index time?
options: The Universal Forwarder always sets it to `syslog`
Automatic source typing
It inherits the value of the target index
It is always tagged `unknown` until manually re-assigned
questions.explanation: Splunk's automatic source typing uses filename patterns via `[source::...]` stanzas, built-in rules for common formats (CSV, JSON, syslog, Apache), and content-analysis fallbacks (`_json`, `_xml`, `generic_single_line`). Option A is wrong — UFs do not blanket-assign `syslog`. Option C confuses sourcetype with index; they are independent. Option D is not a real fallback name in Splunk.

questions.question: Two ways to join results from two searches: `append` and `appendcols`. Which correctly describes `appendcols`?
options: Runs a second search and stacks its rows below the current results, matched by column name
Runs a lookup and appends every column from a CSV to each event that carries the input field
Runs a second search and appends its columns side-by-side, aligned row-by-row
Runs an eval expression and appends its computed column onto every event flowing through
questions.explanation: `appendcols` runs a subsearch and pastes its columns alongside the main results, aligned by row position — missing rows fill with null. Option A describes `append` (row-stacking). Option B describes the `lookup` command. Option D describes `eval`. Only `appendcols` matches the row-aligned columns model.

questions.question: Splunk alerts have two scheduling modes: real-time and scheduled. Which describes them correctly?
options: Real-time = continuous rolling-window (timely, heavy); scheduled = runs on cron
Real-time alerts fire every one second regardless of the rolling-window size chosen
Real-time uses streaming-only evaluation on new events; scheduled evaluates historical data only
Real-time supports email delivery only; scheduled alerts are the only ones with all action types
questions.explanation: A real-time alert continuously evaluates a rolling window (e.g. the last 5 minutes) — most timely, most resource-heavy. Scheduled alerts run the search on a cron cadence and evaluate results after each completion. Option C is wrong — scheduled alerts can search any window including near-real-time. Option B invents a fixed 1-second cadence. Option D limits real-time to email, which is false.

questions.question: An analyst uses `join` to enrich firewall events with user email from an LDAP-backed lookup. What does `join` do, and what is a better alternative?
options: Executes joins entirely on the indexers with zero search-head memory pressure
SQL-style join on a shared field; `lookup` or `stats` is usually faster
Concatenates multivalue fields from both searches, similar to `mvjoin()`
Deprecated in Splunk 8+; the recommended replacement is the `union` command
questions.explanation: `join` runs a subsearch and matches main-result rows to subsearch rows on a shared key — functionally correct but memory-heavy and capped at 50 000 subsearch rows by default. `lookup` (for enrichment from a reference table) or `stats` on a UNION of the two searches (`append + stats`) is usually far cheaper. Option A invents indexer-side execution. Option D is wrong — `join` is fully supported and `union` combines RESULT SETS, not joins. Option C confuses `join` with `mvjoin()`.

questions.question: The time modifier `earliest=-60m@m latest=@m` — what does it evaluate to?
options: From exactly 60 minutes ago (no boundary snap) to the current instant (no boundary snap)
From midnight 60 days ago to midnight of today, using daily boundary snapping
From 60 minutes ago snapped to that minute's start, to the current minute's start
From the start of the current hour to the end of the current hour, using hour snap
questions.explanation: `-60m@m` = 60 minutes ago, then snap back to that minute's :00. `@m` = the start of the current minute. Together they define a clean 60-minute rolling window aligned to minute boundaries — no partial minutes at either edge. Option A ignores the `@m` snap. Option B misreads `m` as days. Option D describes `earliest=@h latest=@h+1h`, not this expression.

questions.question: A team needs 3 years of monthly firewall aggregates without storing 3 years of raw events. Nightly, a search aggregates the day's events and writes summary rows to a dedicated index. Which technique is this?
options: Bucket freezing — moves cold buckets off to slow storage
Report acceleration — pre-builds summaries on the original data
Data-model acceleration — builds tsidx summaries for a data model
Summary indexing
questions.explanation: Summary indexing uses `collect` (or `sistats`/`sichart`) to append aggregated rows to a summary index, so dashboards read a small pre-computed dataset. Report acceleration (B) speeds up ONE report by pre-computing partial results — it does not free you from retaining raw data. Data-model acceleration (C) accelerates data-model queries via tsidx summaries but still relies on raw retention. Bucket freezing (D) is retention lifecycle management, not aggregation.

questions.question: An event has `tags="prod,db,primary"` as a string. To convert it into a multivalue field so per-element commands work, which SPL is idiomatic?
options: `| fields split(tags, ",")` — `fields` cannot call functions on the field list
`| eval tags = split(tags, ",")` — creates a multivalue field from the delimited string
`| mvexpand tags delimiter=","` — `mvexpand` has no `delimiter` argument
`| stats values(tags)` — aggregates unique values across events, not a per-event split
questions.explanation: `eval split(field, delimiter)` returns a multivalue value that can be assigned back to the same field. The `makemv` command does the same job with slightly different syntax (`| makemv delim="," tags`). Option A misuses `fields`, which cannot call functions. Option C is wrong — `mvexpand` takes an already-multivalue field and produces one event per value; it has no delimiter argument. Option D collapses events into an aggregate, which is a different task.

questions.question: An event has multivalue field `users=['alice','bob','carol']`. The analyst wants one row per user (3 rows total). Which SPL command does this?
options: `| makemv users` — converts a string into a multivalue field, not the other way
`| split users by delim=","` — no such SPL command
`| mvexpand users` — one event per multivalue element
`| stats values(users) by _time` — aggregates, does not expand
questions.explanation: `mvexpand <mvfield>` explodes a multivalue field into one event per value, duplicating the rest of the event's fields for each. Option A does the reverse (string → multivalue). Option B is not a real SPL command. Option D collapses events, not expands them. `mvexpand` is the classic pattern for `stats … by <exploded>` on multivalue data.

questions.question: A Splunk data model is a hierarchical knowledge object. Which description is correct?
options: A pre-built ingestion pipeline that normalises CIM-compliant field names during index-time indexing
A saved dashboard template with pre-arranged panels for a given sourcetype family
A visualisation library that renders drill-down charts backed by Splunk saved searches
A hierarchy of datasets with typed fields; drives Pivot and can be accelerated for `tstats`
questions.explanation: A data model organises data into structured datasets (root and child) with typed attributes; it drives Pivot and, when accelerated, stores tsidx summaries queried by `tstats`. Option A confuses data models with CIM add-ons and index-time processing. Option B is a dashboard, not a knowledge object. Option C describes a rendering library, not a schema. Only option D captures the actual data-model definition.

questions.question: An analyst needs a running (cumulative) sum of `bytes` per host, keeping every event but adding the running total as a new field. Which command does this?
options: `| streamstats sum(bytes) AS running_bytes BY host` — running aggregate per event
`| stats sum(bytes) by host` — collapses events into aggregate rows
`| eventstats sum(bytes) AS total_bytes BY host` — same total on every event, not running
`| accum bytes AS running_bytes` — no such SPL command in current Splunk
questions.explanation: `streamstats` computes RUNNING statistics event-by-event in pipeline order, keeping row count unchanged. `stats` (A) collapses to one row per group. `eventstats` (C) appends the SAME (final) aggregate to every event, not a running total. `accum` (D) is not a valid SPL command — the correct running-sum idiom is `streamstats`.

questions.question: Splunk extracts fields in two architectural stages: index-time and search-time. Which describes the trade-off correctly?
options: Both perform equivalently; the distinction is only a documentation label used by Splunk trainers
Index-time runs on the search head at query time; search-time runs on indexers during ingest
Index-time stores fields in the index (fast search, bigger storage); search-time extracts on demand
Index-time is regex-based; search-time only supports key=value pair auto-extraction
questions.explanation: Index-time bakes values into the index — searches are faster but storage grows and mistakes are baked in. Search-time regex runs per query, saving storage at CPU cost, and can be edited without re-indexing. Splunk recommends search-time for almost all cases. Option A denies the whole architectural distinction. Option B swaps the tiers backwards. Option D is wrong — search-time extractions ARE regex-based.

questions.question: An analyst searches for HTTP requests where the URL contains `/admin`. Which SPL pattern is MOST efficient?
options: `index=web | rex "/admin"` — `rex` extracts fields, doesn't filter
`index=web | regex url="/admin"` — post-process regex on every event
`index=web | eval m=if(match(url,"/admin"),1,0) | where m=1` — heavier still
`index=web url=*admin*` — indexed wildcard match in the initial search
questions.explanation: Putting the wildcard match in the initial search clause lets Splunk push the filter to the indexer's lispy engine (bloom filters + bucket elimination). Option B runs `regex` on every event AFTER retrieval, much slower. Option C is even worse — two passes over each event. Option A confuses `rex` (field extraction) with a filter — `rex` doesn't drop non-matching events at all.

questions.question: An analyst wants to bucket `response_ms` into 100-ms-wide bins for a histogram. Which command discretises continuous numeric values into buckets?
options: `| bin span=100 response_ms` — groups values into 100-wide buckets
`| bucket response_ms by 100` — wrong argument syntax for `bucket`/`bin`
`| discretise response_ms span=100` — no such SPL command
`| eval bucket=response_ms/100` — creates a numeric quotient, not a histogram bin
questions.explanation: `bin` (alias `bucket`) discretises continuous numeric or time values into ranges using `span=` (fixed width) or `bins=` (fixed count). `timechart` uses `bin` internally on `_time`. Option B uses invalid `by 100` syntax. Option C is a name-guess. Option D just divides — you'd need to floor/multiply back to align to bucket edges, which is exactly the manual work `bin` avoids.

questions.question: Which is a valid Splunk `eval if(...)` form? Note that `eval` uses `==` for equality.
options: `if(status=200, "OK", "Not OK")` — `=` is assignment/match in `search`, not comparison in `eval`
`if(status==200, "OK", "Not OK")` — canonical comma-separated eval `if`
`if(status=200) then "OK" else "Not OK"` — SPL has no `then/else` keywords
`if status==200 return "OK" else "Not OK"` — no `return` keyword in `eval`
questions.explanation: In `eval`, `if(cond, true_val, false_val)` is comma-separated, and equality comparison requires `==`. Option A is invalid — inside `eval`, `=` is not a comparison; equality is `==`. Options C and D use keyword-based imperative syntax that Splunk does not have. Note that the initial `search` clause uses single-`=` for `field=value` matching — that is a different context from `eval`.

questions.question: SPL has `fields` and `table` for selecting fields. Which correctly describes the difference?
options: `fields` and `table` are exact aliases; the two names exist purely for readability
`table` runs distributed on indexers; `fields` runs only on the search head
`fields` guarantees a fixed column order; `table` does not preserve any order
`table` selects fields AND preserves their column order in the output
questions.explanation: `table <field1, field2, ...>` selects the listed fields AND preserves their left-to-right order in the final result. `fields` (or `fields +`) restricts the pipeline to the listed fields but does NOT enforce column order. Option A is wrong — they differ. Option C reverses the truth. Option B is fabricated — both are pipeline commands.

questions.question: Splunk supports report acceleration: a saved report is registered and Splunk pre-computes partial summaries. Subsequent runs read those summaries. Which describes report acceleration correctly?
options: Pre-computes partial summaries on disk; report must be transforming and scheduled
Report is transpiled into a native binary each night; subsequent runs execute the compiled artefact instead of SPL
Reads accelerated CIM data models directly via `tstats`, bypassing the report definition
Report caches results in RAM for one hour after each run; subsequent runs within that window return instantly
questions.explanation: Report acceleration continuously builds partial summaries on disk for a registered report; future runs read the summaries and only touch raw data for the recent uncovered window. Requirements: the report contains a transforming command, and it runs at least daily. Option D confuses it with a short-lived RAM cache. Option B invents JIT compilation. Option C describes data-model acceleration, which is a different feature — report acceleration is per-report.

questions.question: An analyst runs `| lookup customers customer_id AS user_id OUTPUT name` but gets ZERO matches even though matching rows exist. Most likely cause?
options: The CSV file exceeded the upload size limit and was silently truncated to zero rows
The lookup definition has the input-field/event-field direction inverted, so no rows match
CSV lookups cannot match values containing digits, which excludes numeric IDs like `customer_id`
The lookup was moved to another app and its ACLs no longer apply to the calling search
questions.explanation: The most frequent cause of a 'zero matches' lookup is a name mismatch between the lookup's declared input field and the actual event field. In `lookup customers customer_id AS user_id`, `AS` renames the LOOKUP-side field to match the EVENT-side field — so if the event's field is `user_id`, the CSV must use `customer_id` as its key. Reverse the direction and you get zero matches. Option A is not a silent failure — uploads fail loudly. Option C is false — lookups happily match digits. Option D would produce a permissions error, not zero matches.

questions.question: An analyst wants to plot geo-distributed events on a choropleth or cluster map. Data has `src_ip` and `iplocation` populates lat/lng. Which command aggregates events into the lat/lng grid format consumed by map visualisations?
options: `iplocation` — extracts lat/lng from IP; does not aggregate for maps
`geodistance` — computes distance between coordinates, not a map aggregation
`geostats` — aggregates by lat/lng grid cells for map visualisations
`geomstats` — no such SPL command
questions.explanation: `geostats` is a transforming command that aggregates events into geographic grid cells at the appropriate zoom level, feeding Splunk's map visualisation. Option A is a common upstream step (get lat/lng from IP) but it does NOT aggregate. Option B computes point-to-point distance. Option D is a name-guess.

questions.question: An analyst wants `avg(response_ms) BY host` but wants to KEEP every event and add the per-host average as a new field on each event (to compare each event to the host mean). `stats` collapses to one row per host. Which command preserves events?
options: `eventstats avg(response_ms) AS avg_by_host BY host` — appends the aggregate to every event, no row loss
`streamstats avg(response_ms) AS avg_by_host BY host` — running (cumulative), not final per-host average on every event
`stats avg(response_ms) AS avg_by_host BY host` — collapses to one row per host, the pattern being avoided
`join host [search index=hosts | stats avg(response_ms) by host]` — technically possible but heavier and error-prone
questions.explanation: `eventstats` runs the aggregate ONCE per group and appends the FINAL result to every original event, so `where response_ms > avg_by_host` cleanly picks above-average events. `streamstats` (B) computes running aggregates, so early events get partial averages — not what's wanted. `stats` (C) is the exact pattern we're replacing. Option D is functionally similar but slower, hits the 50 000-row subsearch cap, and duplicates rows on collisions.

questions.question: Which TWO SPL commands are STREAMING commands — they operate per-event and can be distributed to indexers before the search head sees the data?
options: `eval` — computes per-event fields; streaming
`stats` — transforming; must run on the search head after data gathers
`rex` — extracts per-event fields via regex; streaming
`sort` — must see all events; runs on the search head
questions.explanation: `eval` and `rex` both operate on each event independently — they are distributable streaming commands that can run on the indexers before the search head sees data. `stats` and `sort` are transforming commands: `stats` must collect ALL matching events to compute aggregates, and `sort` must see the full result set to order it, so both run on the search head after data gathering completes.
